name: Litefeet

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Litefeet, also referred to as 'getting lite,' is a type of street dance and vernacular dance that emerged from Harlem, New York in the early 2000s and was established in 2006.
The term comes from dancers dancing as though they have 'light feet,' or are weightless.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance has been embraced as a symbol of the urban musical social scene of Harlem.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: TAKE1 - LITE FEET 2019 (https://archive.org/details/ace-rabbit-lite-feet-solo-shot-by-can-iget-asolo-1)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Harlem shake is commonly incorporated into the social dance Litefeet, as is the Chicken Noodle Soup, the Tone Wop, the Rev Up, and the Aunt Jackie.
Additional popular dances include the Bad One and the All In.
Moves often include shuffling, hat tricks, and shoe tricks.
Watch for Harlem shake, Chicken Noodle Soup, Tone Wop.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (fpasBMvRR2E)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: performed on subways in New York City and at Union Square

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Litefeet is also the name of the music played along with the dance, often fast-paced 100-110BPM rap beats and drum kits.

Well-known music producers include LiL LIVE, HANN, M-Lyve, Kid the Wiz, Dsparkz, Fliqht, TweekTune, BSNYEA, H Rockz, Faro, AG the Voice of Harlem, SGFLOW, Lil Sns, Aye Jae Beats, Coma, Lady MoSoFou, DJ Webstar, and Young B.
Listen for the drum kits.
The tempo sits around 105 beats a minute.
Fast-paced 100-110 BPM rap beats paired with drum kits, serving as the musical foundation for Litefeet dancing.
